description: sempods is an open standard and its Kotlin/JVM reference implementation for self-hosted semantic pods: RDF resources addressed as HTTP URIs, every statement in exactly one context (named graph) that is also the permission boundary, and URI-based grants (#read/#write/#manage). Apps reach them over OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code — as static did:web:* clients whose identity is their own HTTPS origin, nothing dereferenced, or as dyn:* clients registered through RFC 7591 DCR, PKCE mandatory for the latter and recommended for the former — while out-of-band service clients use Client Credentials and anonymous callers read a pod's public contexts with no token at all. Adds a read-only SPARQL surface with a server-enforced sandbox, and a /_system/* control plane. Ships the pod server, the identity service, a per-pod MCP endpoint plus a hosted multi-pod MCP service, and JVM client libraries.
rules: sempods is 0.x and the API surface moves, but a large set of names is frozen because each is a contract with something the repository does not control — a deployed host, a database on disk, a published IRI, a registered client. `docs/naming.md` §3 is the authority and lists: every `SEMPODS_*` environment variable; the database names `sempods-server` / `sempods-auth` / `sempods-mcp` and every collection in `SempodsCollections`, `SempodsAuthCollections` and `SempodsMcpCollections`; the ontology IRIs `https://schema.sempods.org/` (12-month deprecation, the project's strongest promise — see `NAMESPACE.md`) and the legacy `https://sempods.org/ontology#`; the `urn:sempods:` prefix behind `urn:sempods:e:<hash>` and `urn:sempods:oidc:<hash>`, which land in stored grants and in the `also_known_as` claim; the media type `application/vnd.sempods.media-source+json`; the MCP identifiers `serverInfo.name` `sempods-mcp`, the DCR `CLIENT_NAME` and the `Bearer realm="sempods-mcp"` challenge; the dev-mode KDF salt in `SecretCipher`; and the deployed infrastructure names — the docker services `sempods-auth` and `sempods-mcp`, the networks and volumes, the S3 buckets and the host paths. One documented exception: the pod server's own docker service `sempods` is *not* frozen. Its name is unsettled on purpose and is pending the pod-resolution seam (`docs/modularity.md` §"Seams that do not exist yet"), so renaming it is a live question rather than a breaking change — it just belongs with that seam and not on its own. Also stable: the refresh-token row shape, the claim names in issued tokens, and the package namespace `org.sempods.*` — `docs/naming.md` §4 calls the packages the wire-adjacent half (KDoc links, logger names, the composition guard) and the namespace is what Maven Central verifies against `sempods.org`, so a package rename is a source- and binary-incompatible break. Freely renameable, by contrast, are Gradle module names and directory names: no directory name appears in any package, which is why `:sempods` → `:sempods-server` and `:sempods-spec` → `:sempods-model` cost zero imports. A module name is deliberately not its package name here — `sempods-server` holds `org.sempods.pods`, `sempods-model` holds `org.sempods.spec`, `org.sempods.ontologies`, `org.sempods.rdf` and `org.sempods.media` — so never propose "fixing" that mismatch. An application built on these modules keeps its own namespace and is not expected to adopt this one. Never propose a consistency rename in the frozen set; it is a breaking change or a data migration, not an edit.

No release exists on Maven Central yet, so never emit a plain `org.sempods:…:0.1.0` — that coordinate does not resolve, and `RELEASING.md` showing it describes the shape a release will take, not one that is available. Snapshots do exist: every merge to `main` publishes the fifteen `publishedModules` plus the `sempods-bom` platform to `https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/`. Consume them by adding that repository and pinning the platform — `implementation(platform("org.sempods:sempods-bom:0.1.0-SNAPSHOT"))`, then module coordinates carrying no version of their own — rather than hand-versioning modules, since one version covers the whole repository and a mixed set is a combination nothing ever ran. Say that a snapshot is mutable, unvalidated, republished on every merge and removed by Central after 90 days. Published bytecode targets Java 21. The coordinates freeze at the first release.

Every statement lives in exactly one context, a named graph identified by its full canonical IRI, and the context is the permission boundary — not the resource, not the property, not a role. There are no project-, app- or role-level abstractions. One resource URI can therefore carry public and private properties at the same time, and a reader sees exactly the depth their grants allow.

Context IRIs live under `/{pod}/_system/contexts/…`. A delegated context carries a type segment (`apps/<id>/…`; `users/…` is reserved for guests); a context the owner keeps carries no type and is named freely. Owner identity never appears in a path — pod ownership is transferable — with guest paths `users/<webid>/…` the deliberate exception.

Grant strings are `<context-iri>#read`, `<context-iri>#write`, `<context-iri>#manage`; `public-read` is a singleton pseudo-scope, not a grant. `#manage` authorizes the context root and its slash-delimited descendants only. Never implement it as a string-prefix check — a sibling context sharing a string prefix must not be authorized. Any grant on a context implies read — the resource layer already makes a `#write` or `#manage` context readable — so never request `#read` alongside `#write` for the same context, and never assume a write-only grant cannot read. The pod owner holds implicit `read | write | manage` on every registered context.

A grant is durable server-side policy and never travels inside a token; scopes are the coarse OAuth capabilities that do. Do not design flows that carry permission topology in a token, and do not treat a token's contents as the authorization decision.

`?context=` exists on the RDF data routes only — the LOD resource path, `_system/resources/{b64url(iri)}` for resources, slots and edges, and `_system/find` as a read downscope. The rest of `/_system/*` is control plane addressed differently and takes no such parameter: a context is created and deleted by its own path at `/{pod}/_system/contexts/{path}` under `#manage`, and DCR at `/{pod}/_system/auth/register` takes a JSON body — never attach `?context=` to either. The MCP write tools carry the target as a `context_iri` argument in JSON instead, one `target` pod and one `context_iri` per call. On the data routes it is required for every write, and the verb set differs by route: `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on a LOD resource and on the `_system/resources/{b64url(iri)}` resource node; `PUT`, `POST` (add a value to a slot) and `DELETE` on a slot; `DELETE` on a single edge. There is no `PATCH` on a slot and no `POST` on a resource node. Every one of them resolves exactly one write context — a missing or repeated `?context=` is 400, and multi-context writes are intentionally not exposed. On reads it is an optional downscope filter: no value means the union of all readable contexts, repetition is allowed, and requested contexts the caller cannot read are silently excluded with no 403, no 404 and no diagnostic header, so context topology never leaks. What an empty result then means depends on the surface: a LOD resource or slot read answers 404, deliberately indistinguishable from "this resource has no statements here"; `GET /{pod}/_system/find` and the MCP `find` tool answer 200 with an empty graph, because an all-unreadable downscope there is a result and not an error.

The SPARQL surface is read-only today and there is no `_system/sparql/update` route — never send a client to one. What exists is `POST /{pod}/_system/sparql/query` and the MCP `sparql_select` / `sparql_graph` tools, all dispatching through one `SparqlQueryService` so the surfaces cannot drift. `validateReadOnly()` parses against the RDF4J grammar and rejects every Update form (INSERT, DELETE, LOAD, CLEAR, CREATE, DROP, COPY, MOVE, ADD) and forbids `SERVICE` anywhere, subqueries included; substring keyword checks are not used, so literals containing keyword tokens are classified correctly. The sandbox is server-enforced and cannot be shaped around: queries see only the caller's readable contexts, and client-supplied dataset clauses are not trusted. Mutations go through the LOD CRUD surface (`PUT` / `PATCH` / `DELETE` with `?context=`) or the `_system/resources/{b64url(iri)}` resource, slot and edge routes.

A `_system` IRI is protected but still describable, and conflating the two costs you the model. Control-plane state — contexts, grants, service-client registrations, the media registry — lives in MongoDB, not in the graph: no amount of RDF about a context IRI alters the context, and deleting a `schema:ImageObject` that names a media URL does not release the bytes. Writing such statements is nonetheless allowed, because the writable *context* is the authorization boundary and never the resource IRI — statements about `did:web:bob.example`, about another pod's resources, and about this pod's own `_system/contexts/apps/notes` are all the same kind of thing: claims, stored wherever the caller may write. Ask `GET {pod}/_system/contexts/{path}` what a context *is* and `GET {pod}/_system/resources/{b64url(iri)}` what anyone has *said about* it; never read the second as the first.

Anonymous is a supported mode on the pod, not a degraded one: with no bearer at all a caller reads the pod's public contexts over the LOD surface and over the pod's own MCP endpoint — never make a client authenticate for a public read there. The hosted multi-pod MCP service is the opposite and must not be described from this rule: it has no anonymous mode, and every id-bearing request (`initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list`, `ping`) needs a valid bearer or gets the 401 OAuth-upgrade challenge; only notifications, which carry no id, are acked without one. Writes and the write tools always require a bearer. Where authentication is required, a bearer that is missing and one that is rejected get the same answer — `401 invalid_token`, which is what `BearerChallenge.forResource` emits for both — while a valid bearer whose scope is not enough is `403 insufficient_scope`. So the absence of a bearer is not an error by itself; it is an error exactly where the operation is not one anonymous callers may perform. A write model parsed from a request must contain statements for the target resource only — smuggled out-of-context triples are rejected.

Client identity has three shapes, not one, and prescribing the wrong one produces a client that cannot connect. `did:web:*` — static clients with a stable HTTPS origin; no DCR and no registration call, because the identity *is* the origin. Nothing is fetched: the identifier is parsed locally, and `did:web:example.org` may simply not redirect anywhere but `https://example.org/…`. A sempods authorization server dereferences nothing here, and an implementation of this contract must not add a step that fetches a DID or client-metadata document — it buys no security and costs an SSRF surface, a cache and a third party in the login path. A non-default port is percent-escaped and further path segments are colon-separated, and the redirect check matches path *segments*: `did:web:example.org:mcp` covers `/mcp` and `/mcp/cb` but not `/mcp-other/cb`, so raw `startsWith` is wrong here for the same reason it is wrong for `#manage`. Loopback redirect URIs are accepted in development only. `dyn:*` — RFC 7591 dynamic clients registered at `POST /{pod}/_system/auth/register`, which is how MCP clients such as Claude Desktop, Copilot and ChatGPT connect; they register with `token_endpoint_auth_method=none`, so PKCE is mandatory, and `/authorize` always renders the consent UI regardless of `prompt` or existing grants (existing grants arrive pre-checked, so the common path is one click). Service clients — registered out-of-band through the host admin surface, never via DCR, and the only clients that may use Client Credentials. Which shape applies is a question about the client's role, not its label. An end-user MCP client such as Claude Desktop has no stable origin of its own and must go through DCR, so never point one at `did:web`. The hosted multi-pod MCP service is the other way round: it *is* a service with an origin, and toward a pod it is an OAuth client that prefers DCR and falls back to `DidWeb.clientId(base)` when that pod advertises no registration endpoint — which is how an RFC 9728-only pod without RFC 8414 discovery gets connected at all, so do not insist on DCR there. Never expect a `dyn:*` client to obtain a service token.

The only user-facing flow is OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code; implicit flow and password grants are not accepted. PKCE is mandatory for `dyn:*` clients and strongly recommended — not required — for `did:web:*` ones: `PodAuthEndpoint` raises the missing-challenge error only when the client id starts with `dyn:`, so do not reject a `did:web` authorization request that carries no `code_challenge`. Where a challenge is present, `S256` is the only accepted method and it is case-sensitive (RFC 7636 §4.3); `plain`, `s256` and an absent method are all refused. Backend services with no user in the loop use the Client Credentials grant (RFC 6749 §4.4), restricted to out-of-band registered service clients. The pod itself is `did:web:<its host>`, and persons are known only as WebID URIs — an email given at pod creation is stored as the WebID derived from it.

There is no schema-migration system. `SempodsUpdater` runs a hardcoded list on every boot with no history and no already-applied check; a failure is logged at error level and boot continues, blocking or not, so an update must be written to be safe when it runs twice or half-ran last time. The one real mechanism is `SempodsUpdate.blocking`: leave it `false` (the default) only for an update that adds data the running system does not read yet — it runs on a daemon thread while the server already serves. Set it `true` as soon as the update changes what existing data *means*, because the surrounding code assumes the new meaning from the first request on; the cost is boot time, since updates run while the injector is built. Before any upgrade: take a backup and read the startup log.

Building it needs Java 25, while published bytecode targets Java 21. Local infrastructure comes up from `deployments/local/compose.yaml` and the server runs via `./gradlew :deployments:sempods:image:run`. The quick start is spelled `docker compose` (Compose v2 plugin) because that is what the README's commands use — but this is a spelling, not a requirement: the standalone `docker-compose` and `podman-compose` both work if the command line is adjusted, so never reject a host for having one of those instead.

Apache-2.0 grants no trademark rights in the name. Accurate descriptive use needs no permission — "compatible with sempods", "implements the sempods specification", "built on sempods" — and relationship names like `acme-pod-client` or `sempods-exporter-for-postgres` are fine. Do not word anything so it implies the project produced or endorsed a third-party build. Two terms are reserved and are the exception: **"sempods conformant"** and **"sempods certified"**, along with rearrangements like "sempods-certified" or "certified for sempods", may be used only under a written licence granted on passing the conformance suite at a stated profile and version. That suite does not exist yet, so nobody can pass it and the terms say nothing — never generate them for an implementation. Write "implements the sempods specification" and document the deviations instead. Five things need permission first, asked at `hello@sempods.org`, where the answer is usually yes: using "sempods" as the name of a product, service, company or organisation or as a distinctive part of one ("SempodsCloud", "Sempods GmbH", "sempods.io"); registering "sempods" or a confusingly similar term as a trademark, company name or domain anywhere; using the project's logo or visual identity as the mark of your own offering; any presentation suggesting your work *is* the project, is its official version, or is endorsed by it; and naming a fork "sempods" or a close variant — a fork may say what it derives from, it may not occupy the name.
